app.title: National land-cover change and carbon accounting by district (Streamlit)
app.summary: The person picks a region from a national, territory and district hierarchy and a pair of epochs to compare. The app reads cached per-district class areas and from-to transition tables, and builds several views from them. It shows a live classified map for any year, headline area and carbon-stock changes with low, best and high bounds, the flow of land between classes, trajectories over all epochs, and a worked step-by-step version of the arithmetic. At the end it ranks every district by built-up gain and carbon change, and the person can download the conversion table or the district table as CSV.

task.text: Estimate how much terrestrial carbon a region gained or lost through land-cover conversions between two dates, with an uncertainty band, and find the districts where it changed most.

data.text: Classified land-cover rasters at several epochs, reduced to per-district class areas and from-to transition areas. These are combined with a per-class table of carbon densities, each given as low, best and high.
data.item: an administrative district's class areas at one epoch and its class-to-class transition areas between two epochs

stage.text: computing carbon change from an existing land-cover classification and comparing regions and periods, before write-up

mechanism.text: Sidebar selectors for region, epoch pair, map year and class scheme drive every tab at once. Each tab turns the same cached tables into a different view: a tiled map, metric cards with a flow diagram and a ranked conversion chart, stacked trajectories, a printed worked calculation, and a district scatter with ranked tables and CSV export.

field.text: land-cover change and area-times-density carbon accounting from satellite classification, in remote sensing

workflow.name: estimate change in a quantity from class transitions between two dates, by region

steps.here: Per-district class areas and transition crosstabs are loaded from a cache that was built once from Earth Engine. A warning appears while any epoch is still incomplete.

steps.step: choose the region and the two dates to compare
steps.here: The person picks a region (country, territory, then optionally a district) and an epoch pair. The pair labels show the requested year against the map year actually used, and flag pairs that cross the product seam or are seam-free.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: A tiled classified map can be set to any archive year with a slider and switched between the full legend and four classes. It shows the region's outline and a legend.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Areas are multiplied by per-class carbon densities to give stocks. Each from-to conversion is scored as area × (destination density − origin density). The results are gross loss, gross gain and net with low and high bounds, and the vegetation-to-built-up conversion is reported separately.
A flow diagram shows conversions between the two epochs. Ranked bars show the largest losses and gains. Stacked area, grouped-bar and carbon-band charts cover all epochs.

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: Every district is plotted as built-up gain against net carbon change. Top-10 tables list the largest expansion and the largest loss, and a full table is sorted by carbon change.
The full conversion table for the chosen region and pair, and the district table, download as CSV.

distinctive: Every density is a low/best/high triple carried through each sum. The flux band pairs the poorest destination with the richest origin, and a warning appears whenever a band crosses zero.
Comparisons that cross a seam between two production lines of the source product are flagged, and a seam-free baseline is the default.
An unreliable class (snow read as permanent ice) gets its share of gross loss computed, and net flux is reported with and without it.
A 'show the arithmetic' tab prints the reduction code, the density table and the actual multiplications. It also measures how far an older single-density table would have been off.
Regions are an exact sum of districts accounted at native resolution, and the disputed territories that have no districts are carried as whole units.
